https://business-review.eu/business/huma.text: Over 40% of Romanian employees aged 55+ express willingness to work beyond retirement age – study More than four in ten Romanian employees aged 55 and over are willing to continue working beyond the statutory retirement age, compared with approximately one-third of their European counterparts, according to a study by HR solutions provider SD Worx. The findings also suggest that older Romanian workers report higher job satisfaction, stronger engagement, and greater confidence in their professional abilities than younger employees. In Romania, 42% of employees aged 55 and over say they would be willing to work beyond retirement age, compared with 32% across Europe. Among Romanian employees under 35, the proportion stands at 34%, also above the European average of just over 25%. The findings come as Europe’s workforce continues to age. According to Eurostat data cited in the study, people aged 65 and over accounted for 17% of Europe’s population in 2005, with their share estimated to reach 22% in 2025. The European Commission projects that the EU workforce will shrink by approximately 12% between 2022 and 2070, despite higher labour market participation among older workers and women. Labour shortages are already affecting employers, with 49% of Romanian HR decision-makers reporting difficulties finding staff, compared with 52% across Europe. Older employees report higher job satisfaction and less interest in early retirement Read more about Romanians travel the shortest distance on their daily commute compared with other Europeans but spend nearly 53 minutes on the road read more The study found that 40% of Romanian employees aged 55 and over would prefer early retirement, compared with 63% of those under 35. Across Europe, the corresponding figures are approximately 50% and 61%. For older Romanian employees considering early retirement, the main motivations are spending more time with family or pursuing personal interests (78%), health concerns (72%), and achieving personal goals (44%). Lower motivation at work was cited by 36%, while physical and psychological demands were mentioned by 13% and 17%, respectively. Older employees also expressed more positive views about their current working lives. Some 86% of Romanian respondents aged 55 and over believe they have enough energy to perform their jobs well, compared with 76% across Europe. Meanwhile, 84% said their work gives them a sense of purpose and fulfilment, compared with 69% of Romanian employees under 35. Overall job satisfaction was also higher among older workers, at 84%, compared with 72% among younger employees. Similarly, 74% of those aged 55 and over felt appreciated at work, versus 64% of their younger colleagues. Career mobility and training interest decline with age Older Romanian employees are considerably less likely to seek a new position. Only 9% of workers aged 55 and over are actively looking for a job with another employer, compared with 32% of those under 35. The same proportion of older employees, 9%, are seeking a different role within their current organisation, versus 25% of younger workers. The generational differences also extend to professional development. Among Romanian employees aged 55 and over, 46% say they are not interested in participating in training programmes, compared with 32% of those under 35. However, 63% of older employees still want to develop their skills further, compared with 77% of younger workers. Both figures exceed the corresponding European averages of 58% and 70%. Older workers express greater job security despite lower AI adoption Romanian employees aged 55 and over are more confident about their job security in the face of automation than their younger colleagues. Some 64% feel secure in their roles even as automation changes their tasks, compared with 51% of workers under 35. Regular use of artificial intelligence tools is less widespread among older employees, however. Only 30% of Romanian workers aged 55 and over use AI regularly in their daily activities, compared with 42% of younger employees. Both figures exceed European averages of 20% and 38%, respectively. The study also found that 67% of Romanian employees aged 50 and over believe their human skills cannot be replaced by AI, compared with 69% of those under 35. Despite relatively high confidence in their abilities, employees report limited organisational support in adapting to AI. Only 31% of Romanian workers aged 55 and over believe they receive sufficient support to prepare for an AI-driven workplace, compared with 35% of younger employees. The corresponding European averages are 17% and 29%. The findings highlight the potential contribution of older employees to addressing labour shortages, while also pointing to the need for employers to adapt training and workforce development strategies to different age groups.
